- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $f(x)={sin}^{5}⁡x$ is an odd function, but integral I is not of the form ${\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x$ since the upper and lower limits are not opposites. Therefore, we cannot use symmetry to simplify the integral.

$$

$$

{\int }_{-2}^{2}({x}^{3}+{x}^{5})\,\text{d}x=0.

$$

A linear transformation $T$ satisfies two properties:

$$
\begin{aligned} & T\begin{bmatrix}kx \\ ky\end{bmatrix}=kT\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}, \\  & T\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}=T\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+T\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Checking the first condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T\begin{bmatrix}kx \\ ky\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}(kx)^{2} \\ 7(ky)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{k}^{2}({x}^{2}) \\ k(7y)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =k\begin{bmatrix}k({x}^{2}) \\ 7y\end{bmatrix} \\  & \ne kT\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{T}$ is not a linear transformation.

- Checking the second condition, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}T\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2})^{2} \\ 7({y}_{1}+{y}_{2})\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2} \\ 7{y}_{1}+7{y}_{2}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}^{2} \\ 7{y}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2}^{2} \\ 7{y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{1}{x}_{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =T\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+T\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2{x}_{1}{x}_{2} \\ 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & \ne T\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {y}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+T\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{2} \\ {y}_{2}\end{bmatrix}.\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

As a result, only statement III is true.

$$

$$
det(A)=\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1\end{vmatrix}=1\cdot (-1)-2\cdot 1=-3.

A connected region $D$ is simply connected if every simple closed curve in $D$ can be contracted to a point.

![](images/7d/7d6aea1a62fb290702630ef95ec86f4119e7c8fdd74b8148b62b66e5ac871b58.png)

A connected *plane* region $D$ is simply connected if every simple closed curve in $D$ encloses only points in $D.$ In other words, the region does not contain any holes. Plane regions containing holes are not simply connected, since some simple closed curves cannot be contracted to a point:

![](images/c3/c3c3e7a60ff0dd917cf6c0b293dae7510e457a0455629add1c54cadac65248b7.png)

- Region I is simply connected. Indeed, it is the half-plane $y\ge x.$ So,   it's a plane region without holes,

- Region III is *not* simply connected. The region contains all the points of ${R}^{2}$ except those on the straight line $y=-x.$ Thus, the region is formed by two disjoint half-planes and, therefore, is not even a connected region.

\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,y={x}^{4}}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}}{{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}\sqrt{{x}^{4}}}{{x}^{4}+({x}^{4})^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}\cdot {x}^{2}}{{x}^{4}+{x}^{8}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2{x}^{4}}{{x}^{4}(1+{x}^{4})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2\cancel{{x}^{4}}}{\cancel{{x}^{4}}(1+{x}^{4})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\,\frac{2}{1+{x}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{2}{1+{0}^{4}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $x=0$” is true. Taking $x\to (0,0)$ along the path $x=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (0,0)\,\,\,x=0}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}}{{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}} & ={lim}_{y\to 0}\frac{2({0}^{2})\sqrt{y}}{{0}^{4}+{y}^{2}} \\  & ={lim}_{y\to 0}0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement “The limit does not exist” is true. Because the limit evaluates to different results on two different paths, we conclude that the limit does not exist:

$$
{lim}_{x\to (0,0)}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}\sqrt{y}}{{x}^{4}+{y}^{2}}=\text{DNE}
$$
The limit evaluates to $4$ along the path $y={x}^{4}$
The limit evaluates to $0$ along the path $x=0$
The limit does not exist
